content.thinking:
I'm thinking through a whimsical capybara design, scaling up its rounded barrel body, blocky snout, and sleepy expression while shrinking its legs, then adding a tiny cheerful bird perched on its head for extra charm.

I'm now planning the actual proportions and spatial layout—sketching coordinates for the body, head, and legs relative to a standing capybara, then setting up a skeleton with a hip root and spine chain to support the pose.

The region before the hips joint should just get owned by that first joint, so I'll leave the rump loft coverage there. I'll give the capybara a minimal tail stub, just a single tiny "tail1" joint off the hips, and start planning the front legs from the shoulder points around x ±0.14, y 0.3, z 0.25 using a limb bone setup.

Planning leg joint naming for left/right sides with shoulder-elbow-hand chains, then figuring out toe structure—using small capsule rods or sprout joints for front feet's four toes and hind feet's three toes, attached at the foot tip.

I'll use the sole option for the front limb, with 3 segments (shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand) so the final tube points forward horizontally like a paw, and have toes sprout from that paw endpoint.

For hind legs, I'll structure hip-knee-hock-paw with the hock solved by the sole constraint, leaving knee as the single forward bend in a 2-bone IK setup. Now I'm shaping the capybara's barrel body with taller hips, using lofted stations to control width and height along the spine.

Now I'm shaping the head with a chunky, whimsical capybara look — tall blunt snout, high-set small eyes and ears, nostrils on top. I'm lofting the head profile from skull back to snout tip with stations defining width and height at each depth point.

The upper snout is rounded via a circular cross-section loft, with a separate smaller lofted lower jaw tucked beneath. I'm layering on cute details: a flattened dark nose pad with big nostrils, a painted mouth line, rosy cheek spots, decal eyes with highlights, thin whisker tubes, and two cream buck teeth for extra charm.

Now I'm working out the rig: a jaw joint aimed forward, a lower jaw capsule bound to a jaw bone, and a neck joint bridging the body spine to the head joint so the whole chain connects smoothly from hips through neck to head.

I'm settling on the hips root joint feeding into the spine chain, following the docs pattern of bone ordering like tail, hips, spine, head for the loft. The head and body will be separate meshes with the head rigid on its own joint while the body skins to the spine, blending smoothly at the neck overlap.

For ears I'm placing small rounded flattened spheres with pink interiors high on the back of the head at roughly (±0.1, 0.55, 0.47), each rigged to its own hinge joint off the head. Then I'm designing a whimsical little bird perched between the ears at the top of the head — cream belly, blue back, orange-red cheeks, yellow beak, tiny tail, extruded feather wings, and small legs.

For the bird's legs I'm adding orange gripping feet and setting up its own joint hierarchy (birdRoot parented to head, with hinges for wings, tail, beak, and legs), keeping it facing forward in the same direction as the capybara for a clean side silhouette. I'm sizing it like a chubby robin, about 0.14 long with a body radius of 0.045.

Now I'm working out the body geometry: a scaled sphere for the torso with countershading (dark back, cream belly), a separate smaller sphere for the head, and cone shapes for the upper and lower beak pointing forward.

Now I'm planning the capybara's fur coloring: a warm tawny-brown coat with darker grain streaks, countershaded against a lighter belly, a darker muzzle, black nose, and pink cheek accents for a cheerful whimsical look, plus scattered fur tufts for texture.

For the tufts, I'm sketching a simple three-strand grey tuft shape tinted by the coat color, scattering a few hundred cards across the body with spacing around 0.045-0.05 to keep density reasonable (~350-450 cards), leaning them back for a natural flow. I'm also considering small whimsical extras like a flower accent before deciding to keep things simple.

For the daisy, I'll add a tiny pink daisy tucked behind the capybara's ear as a charming accessory, built cheaply with a ring of eight petal cards. Now I'm setting foot contact so the toes rest right at floor level.

Positioning the eyes high on the sides of the head using surface decals, with a dark pupil, two highlights, and a sleepy lash line for that cute expression, placed via azimuth/elevation on the head surface.

For nostrils and the nose pad, I'm figuring out where the capybara's blunt snout tip should sit and shaping a flattened dark cap there, using nearest-surface hits rather than decals to get the geometry right.

Now I'm thinking through the mouth: a smiling closed-lip line draped as a curved polyline on each cheek, plus a soft pink blush ellipse near the mouth corners for charm.

For whiskers, I'll add three thin tube sweeps per side extending outward from points near the snout sides, keeping them dark and slender. Then for the teeth, I'm placing two small cream rounded boxes just under the upper lip at the snout front to suggest visible incisors.

Now I'm working out the lower jaw placement, positioning it to sit behind and below the upper snout so the chin shows naturally beneath the muzzle, adjusting the center height and thickness so it overlaps the head base without looking disconnected.

I'm adding cream-colored teeth boxes placed at the front edge of the upper snout, slightly inset to peek from under the lip, and thinking about overall proportions—making the head a bit generously sized relative to the body for a whimsical look.

For the feet, I'm planning chubby whimsical toes with dark nail accents, three toes on the hind feet and four in front, and darkening the feet color via a gradient that transitions from the coat color to a darker brown near the ground.

For the body surface, I'm layering a countershaded coat: a fine grain pattern running along the z-axis combined with mottling on the belly, nested so the back and belly use different paint treatments. For the head, I'm adding a darker muzzle and snout top using gradients and conditional paint based on position.

For texture details, I'm thinking about adding small fur tufts — finer cheek fluff and a whimsical cowlick between the ears where the bird perches.

Now I'm settling the bird's palette: a bluebird-robin hybrid with blue back (#4fa3e8), orange breast (#ffb25a), cream belly, yellow-orange beak, and darker orange legs for contrast. I'm planning the wing geometry as an extruded feather outline running along the back axis, with darker primary feathers at the tips.

Working out the extrude orientation vectors so the thickness direction points outward correctly, computing the cross product of the x and y axes to confirm it points along +X, then adjusting y slightly to tilt the wing outward.

Now I'm shaping the bird's body as a stretched sphere with a smaller head sphere merging above-front, plus a little crest tuft of spikes, and setting up joints for head, tail, jaw, and wings. For the tail I'm sketching a rounded feather-fan outline to extrude along a bone, angled slightly upward and flattened horizontally.

Working out the plane normal for the tail extrusion so it lies flat with the right orientation, then fanning out three feathers at slight yaw angles with blue bodies and dark tips. I'm positioning the bird on top of the capybara's head, estimating where the tail should extend relative to the body's z-position.

Now I'm starting to write the actual Three.js scene code, importing the builder and frame utilities to construct the joint hierarchy precisely.

Defining the skeleton joints...

Adding more joints...

Still working out leg geometry...

Confirming the last limb segment ends exactly at the target, so the paw naturally forms from wrist to tip. Now I'm planning the toe sprouts: four small tubes splayed across the foot tip, offset in x with slight forward and outward angles, each anchored to the foot's end frame and named uniquely per leg.

So the root frame should be the hand's tip joint at the paw end, with the toe's path prefixed from that point and fanning forward with splayed x-offsets, tube radii tapering with round caps.

I need to check the toe radius so the foot bottom actually touches the floor rather than hovering — adjusting the radius slightly so it sits flush. For nails, I'll add a small dark cone at each toe tip using a spike helper anchored to the toe joint's tip position and direction.

Since capybara nails are blunt and hoof-like rather than pointed, I'm reconsidering using a flattened sphere nail instead of a sharp spike, positioned slightly forward of the toe tip with a squashed scale to mimic a stubby nail shape.

Actually, a cheaper approach: rather than adding a separate nail mesh, I could just color the toe tube using banded gradients along its length, with the final section shifted to a dark nail color. That's simpler and still reads well visually, so I'll use that instead. Now I'm thinking through the head loft geometry with its own bone chain and circular cross-sections, plus whether to add cheek puff details.

I'm adding small flattened cheek spheres bound to the head bone, keeping them the same paint as the head so they blend seamlessly, and working out the snout shape so it has a tall, blunt, domed tip like a capybara's nose, with a darker nose pad on the front face.

Working out the loft cap geometry so the muzzle ends with a squared-off, slightly rounded front instead of an awkward pointed dome, adjusting station widths and heights near the tip to get that whimsical blocky capybara snout look.

I'll finalize the stations tapering toward a flat .17x.20 end cap at z .995, with a small dark nose-pad sphere sitting proud on the front. Then checking the head's back cap placement to make sure its round dome tucks inside the body rather than poking through, comparing widths at the overlap point.

Still adjusting the loft stations...

Wait, totaling the length from rump to snout gives 1.65m, way too long for a realistic capybara which should be around 1.25m. I need to compress the z-coordinates: shrinking the body span down to roughly -0.5 to 0.72 and rescaling the head/snout proportions accordingly.

Writing spine and joint coordinates...

Continuing the head stations through the snout end at z.70, where the total body length works out to about 1.23 meters. I'm placing the eyes near the top of the head around z.47, and figuring out ear positions behind the eyes at the top corners of the skull.

Adding a bird perched on top of the head, sized and positioned so it clears the ears with enough margin, bringing the total height up to about .62. Now I'm starting the jaw geometry, setting the joint and aim points and beginning the lower jaw loft stations.

Repositioning the nose pad to sit higher at the top of the front face where a capybara's nostrils would be, with small dark dents for nostrils and a thin split line running down from the pad to suggest the upper lip crease, plus planning a mouth line drape across the face.

Adding blush decals with soft pink ellipses and tiny freckle dots, then sketching thin whisker tubes as swept polylines on each side of the snout.

For the eyes, I'm designing a dark sclera circle with layered highlight dots for sparkle, topped with a sleepy half-closed eyelid arc in a darker coat tone to give the capybara its calm expression.

For placement, I'm working out the decal positioning on the head surface, figuring out the point coordinates and direction vector so the eye texture wraps naturally and mirrors correctly for the opposite side.

Now I'm moving on to ears, thinking through using a flattened sphere primitive scaled along its axes and oriented with an aim direction to get a rounded ear shape attached to an ear bone joint.

Still arranging the daisy petals...

For fur tufts on the body, I'm scattering cards across the body sweep where hits carry bones from the skin, and designing a grayscale tuft texture with a central blade and two side blades in white and light gray so the coat paint color can tint it. I'm setting the card flow direction toward the back with a small size and symmetric lean, since the tuft shape itself is already symmetric.

Now I'm planning body coverage at around 380 cards with a minimum distance filter excluding the underside, keeping triangle cost manageable at roughly 6k total, and setting up a smaller head scatter of 90 cards that filters out the snout and front face area so fur tufts stay on the cheeks and back of the head rather than covering eyes or decals.

I'm refining that head filter to carve out a ring of cheek tufts on either side of the face, using position bounds on z and y plus an x-offset check to avoid the mouth line, with roughly 14 cards per side at a tight minimum distance.

Then I consider a tail nub, sketching a small capsule bone from roughly the rear of the body tapering down and back, but reconsider since capybaras don't really have a visible tail -- deciding it's more anatomically honest to skip it entirely rather than add a whimsical nub. Moving on, I start setting up the bird part with a root "birdBody" joint parented to the head.

Placing the bird's skeleton: body and head joints stacked near the top, a jaw joint for the lower beak, wing joints angled outward on each side, a tail joint pointing back, and tiny leg joints beginning to take shape near the base.

Now I'm double-checking sizing against the head surface, adjusting the body center and radius so the bird's feet land realistically on the perch without sinking too far below the surface, even if the legs end up mostly hidden under the body.

Working out the bird body geometry — a scaled sphere elongated into an ellipsoid shape, positioned and tilted to tip the tail slightly upward using an X-axis rotation.

Placing the head sphere just above and in front of the body center so it blends naturally, bringing the total bird height to roughly .67 once a crest tuft is added, and starting the beak as a small cone jutting out from the head.

Sketching the upper and lower beak as orange-yellow cones of different sizes, then adding tiny dark eye spheres with small white highlight dots, a rosy cheek blush, and now moving on to shading the breast with cream and orange countershading.

Still defining bird paints...

I'm deciding to skip sharp-corner smoothing concerns for now and just test it visually. Then I'm working out where the wing attaches to the sphere body, checking the body's width tapers near the wing's y-span so the wing plate sits embedded correctly rather than floating off the surface, and figuring out the tilt angle for the wing's plane.

Next I'll add small crest spikes near the bird's head, fanning backward from a point near the top, plus plan the tail with three feather shapes.

Writing feather outline coordinates...

Adding toe details for the bird's feet, then thinking about small character touches like beak expression before deciding against extra props. I'm now setting up the capybara's fur color palette, keeping track of the flat color count to stay within the 64-color limit.

Finalizing the whimsical coat tones, then planning a darker dorsal stripe along the spine using a custom gradient paint for subtle countershading.

Defining more paint layers...

Skipping thigh fur cards, I'm working out the leg sweep geometry with tapered radii along the chain and positioning toe segments at the paw tip.

Now I'm working out the hind leg geometry, placing the hip root and foot target so the two upper segments can bend forward naturally to reach a heel position behind and below the body, then extending the toes forward from there. I'm shifting to positioning the front leg root next.

I'm also tallying up the full joint count across hips, spine, neck, head, ears, and all four legs with their toe segments, landing around fifty total, and starting to assign unique names like shoulderL/elbowL/wristL/handL for the front legs and hipL/kneeL/hockL for the hind.

Writing toe sprout logic...

Paint detail stays low-frequency by default, so texel density isn't a major concern. I'm sketching the eye texture as an SVG with a dark iris ellipse, white highlight circles, and an upper eyelid shape covering the top.

Still refining eyelid curve...

I'm adding happy brow accents and sizing the eye decal small, then layering cheek blush with freckle dots in pink and darker tones. Now I'm sketching a grayscale tuft shape using layered paths for a soft furry highlight effect.

For the coat color I'm setting up a Paint read once at root so cards get tinted consistently. I'm now positioning whiskers emerging from the muzzle near the nose, computing start and tip coordinates for thin rod shapes on each side.

I'm deciding whiskers should droop slightly using a quadratic bezier curve through three points rather than a straight rod, and planning to write the bird as its own function while keeping everything in one file organized by section, mostly using world coordinates with explicit head bone direction for orientation.

Adding nose and nostril details...

Now I'm working out the mouth geometry — a thin dark rod for the philtrum split, then plotting a path of points along the jaw to form the lip-line sweep, making sure each point drapes onto the nearest surface of the head so the smile curve follows the face contour correctly.

Writing skeleton setup code...

Now I'm setting sides to 12 for a smoother body, then moving on to building the legs with a gradient from coat to foot color and limb points for each side, figuring out how the chain function should take the polyline and attach to the correct parent joint for the shoulder.

Mapping out which spine segment each leg chain should parent to—front legs off spine3, hind legs off the hips—and naming the joints shoulder/elbow/wrist/hand with a "leg" role, then sweeping the chain with varying radii using the leg gradient paint.

Now I'm sprouting toe digits off each hand tip, splaying four toes outward along the x-axis with slight offsets and a forward-downward taper, coloring them with footpad and nail bands.

Then I'm lofting the head and jaw shapes from their station curves, adding flat-capped tube geometry with 10-12 sides and a separate color for cheeks and jaw.

For eyes I'm decaling the texture onto the skull sweep, and wrapping the body in a surface so I can scatter fur cards across it, filtering out ones where the normal points too far downward so legs and undersides stay clean. I think I've worked through enough of the rig details now, so it's time to actually write the file.
